第 14 章 Define Your Culture Before It Defines Itself在文化自我定义之前先定义它

Mike Pappas / 迈克·帕帕斯

— 第 49 页 —

In school, I studied physics and applied mathematics. I spent a long time thinking about formulae and systems, analyzing data, and generally trying to quantify anything in sight.

上学时，我学的是物理和应用数学。我花了很长时间思考公式和系统、分析数据，基本上是想量化眼前的一切。

I tend to bring that attitude into how I think about leading a company. Metrics are important, both to discover strengths and weaknesses and to communicate the state of things.

我倾向于把这种态度带入我领导公司的方式中。指标很重要，既用来发现优缺点，也用来传达现状。

Culture naturally resists quantitative metrics. (Not to say metrics don't exist—there are a few—but none without fairly obvious gaps.) Because of this, I dismissed the importance of culture when I was still in school and merely speculating about what working at a company would be like.

文化天然地抗拒量化指标。（不是说不存在指标——有那么几个——但没有一个不存在明显的漏洞。）正因如此，我在上学时还在想象公司工作是什么样的时候，就忽略了文化的重要性。

Fast forward to today, and I haven't really learned much to help me quantify the importance of culture. But nonetheless, I've been convinced.

快进到今天，我并没有学到多少能帮我量化文化重要性的东西。但尽管如此，我已经被说服了。

Culture is really, really important.

文化真的、真的很重要。

What do I mean when I say culture? It's a bit fuzzy, but here's how I think about it:

我说的文化是什么意思？有点模糊，但我是这么理解的：

A company's product is the what. Their customers are the why. Their employees are the who. Culture is the how.

公司的产品是「做什么」。客户是「为什么」。员工是「谁」。文化是「怎么做」。

This is a pretty large claim. There's a lot in the "how" that might not traditionally be considered culture. But ultimately, culture is about people, and that's what all questions of "how" boil down to: how do the people in the company operate?

这是一个很大的说法。「怎么做」里有很多东西传统上可能不被认为是文化。但归根结底，文化是关于人的，而所有「怎么做」的问题最终都归结于此：公司里的人是怎么运作的？

The fact that culture is inherently fuzzy makes it crucial to define clearly what yours is all about. This probably sounds obvious, but I've seen far too many companies end up using something like the following:

文化本质上是模糊的，这使得明确定义你的文化到底是什么至关重要。这听起来可能很明显，但我见过太多公司最后用的是类似这样的话：

— 第 50 页 —

We're world-class technologists excited to work on world-changing problems. We care deeply for one another and are united by our desire to make the world a better place.

我们是世界级的技术人员，热衷于从事改变世界的问题。我们彼此深切关怀，因让世界变得更美好的愿望而团结在一起。

Now tell me, how much have you really learned from that? And, what's more, what kinds of employees are being selected for by a paragraph like this?

现在告诉我，你从这段话里真正了解到了多少？而且，这样一段话在筛选什么样的员工？

In information theory, information is defined as, roughly, the degree to which one's uncertainty is reduced when they receive it. So, given that definition, my problem with paragraphs like those you just read is that they convey almost no actual information.

在信息论中，信息大致被定义为一个人接收到它时不确定性减少的程度。那么，根据这个定义，我对上面那种段落的问题是：它们几乎不传达任何实际信息。

This is bad for two reasons. First, this nondescription will fail to separate your company from the pack—and you need to be different to succeed. But, even more dangerously, the risk here is that, by effectively opting out of defining your culture, you're leaving your actual culture up to chance.

这很糟糕，有两个原因。第一，这种什么都没说的描述无法让你的公司脱颖而出——而你需要与众不同才能成功。但更危险的是，风险在于：你实际上选择了不定义你的文化，就是在把你真正的文化交给运气。

With language like this, which doesn't offend or raise disagreements with anybody but also conveys no information, you're likely to find a scattered set of candidates, with very different expectations, coming into your organization. They might all be great in their own ways, but without shared expectations, they'll inevitably clash, and the aspects that eventually win out to become part of your culture will be decided simply by which random types of people join your company earlier on.

用这种不得罪人、也不引起分歧但同时不传达任何信息的语言，你可能会招来一群期望差异巨大、五花八门的候选人进入你的组织。他们各自可能都很优秀，但没有共同的期望，他们不可避免地会冲突，而最终胜出成为你文化一部分的那些东西，将仅仅由哪些随机类型的人更早加入你的公司来决定。

If you believe as I do that a good culture can be the difference between success and failure, this should terrify you. And the only way to avoid it is to define your culture at the outset—and do it in a way that conveys information. This means defying someone's expectations—which means there will be people out there who disagree.

如果你像我一样相信好的文化可能是成功与失败的分水岭，这应该让你感到恐惧。而避免它的唯一方法是在一开始就定义你的文化——而且是以传达信息的方式来定义。这意味着违背某些人的期望——也就是说会有人不同意。

It's OK to say, "You're a great candidate but not a good fit for our culture!" That's not a value judgement of a candidate. Companies do have different cultures, and often in ways that meaningfully affect someone's happiness. Some people just want to crush on difficult problems and are totally fine working 12-hour days. Other people deliver the best results not through 12-hour days but through shorter work days allowing for more rest and inspiration. It would be nice to be able to accept any candidates, and give them each the experience best suited for them, but the reality is that this can't always happen.

说「你是个很好的候选人，但和我们的文化不太匹配」是可以的。这不是对候选人的价值判断。公司确实有不同的文化，而且往往以深刻影响一个人幸福感的方式不同。有些人就是想攻克难题，每天工作 12 小时完全没问题。另一些人不是通过每天 12 小时工作而是通过更短的工作日获得更多休息和灵感来交付最好的结果。能接受所有候选人、给每个人最适合的体验当然好，但现实是这不一定总是能做到。

Your culture definitely needs to be able to accommodate certain kinds of differences from yourself—no company will succeed without a diversity of ideas and backgrounds—but if there's a real, meaningful culture difference, it's crucial to be able to detect, explain, and act on it.

你的文化当然需要能够容纳和你不同的某些类型——没有思想和背景的多样性，没有公司能成功——但如果存在真正的、有意义的文化差异，能够发现、解释并据此采取行动就至关重要。

— 第 51 页 —

The bottom line is simple: until you can crisply imagine turning away a world-class candidate because they don't match the culture you're building, you haven't yet defined your culture at all.

底线很简单：直到你能清晰地想象因为一个世界级候选人和你正在建设的文化不匹配而拒绝他，你才真正定义了你的文化。
